title: Formal Charges and Resonance
lead: When more than one Lewis structure can be written for a molecule or ion, formal charges help us decide which is the most reasonable. The formal charge of each atom in a Lewis structure is easy to calculate, and four guidelines choose among possible structures. In resonance, the actual distribution of electrons is an average of two or more Lewis structures.
objectives: Compute formal charges for atoms in any Lewis structure
Use formal charges to identify the most reasonable Lewis structure for a given molecule
Explain the concept of resonance and draw Lewis structures representing resonance forms for a given molecule
summary_html: In a Lewis structure, formal charges can be assigned to each atom by treating each bond as if one-half of the electrons are assigned to each atom. These hypothetical formal charges are a guide to determining the most appropriate Lewis structure. A structure in which the formal charges are as close to zero as possible is preferred. Resonance occurs in cases where two or more Lewis structures with identical arrangements of atoms but different distributions of electrons can be written. The actual distribution of electrons (the resonance hybrid) is an average of the distribution indicated by the individual Lewis structures (the resonance forms).

exercises.prompt:
Write resonance forms that describe the distribution of electrons in each of these molecules or ions.
(a) selenium dioxide, OSeO
(b) nitrate ion, ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$
(c) nitric acid, HNO3 (N is bonded to an OH group and two O atoms)
(d) benzene, C6H6:

(e) the formate ion:

answer.solution: For each species, count the valence electrons and write one Lewis structure with the section’s procedure, keeping the arrangement of atoms given. Then look for a double bond that could equally well be drawn to another atom of the same kind: moving only that pair of electrons, with the lone pairs that go with it, gives each further resonance form. Join the forms with double-headed arrows, as for the nitrite and carbonate ions, and check that every form has the same atoms in the same places and the same total charge.

exercises.prompt: Write the resonance forms of ozone, O<sub>3</sub>, the component of the upper atmosphere that protects the Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

answer.solution: Count the valence electrons of three oxygen atoms and write a Lewis structure with one oxygen atom in the center. The central atom reaches an octet only if one of its two bonds is a double bond, and nothing makes one terminal oxygen atom different from the other, so the double bond may be drawn to either. The two structures, joined by a double-headed arrow, are the resonance forms, as the two forms of the nitrite ion are.

exercises.prompt: Sodium nitrite, which has been used to preserve bacon and other meats, is an ionic compound. Write the resonance forms of the nitrite ion, ${\text{NO}}_{\text{2}}{}^{\text{–}}\text{.}$

In terms of the bonds present, explain why acetic acid, CH3CO2H, contains two distinct types of carbon-oxygen bonds, whereas the acetate ion, formed by loss of a hydrogen ion from acetic acid, only contains one type of carbon-oxygen bond. The skeleton structures of these species are shown:

answer.solution: Complete the Lewis structure of each species from its skeleton. In acetic acid, one oxygen atom also carries the hydrogen atom, so only the other oxygen atom can take the double bond. Only one structure can be written, with one single C–O bond and one double bond. In the acetate ion, the two oxygen atoms are bonded alike, and the double bond may go to either of them. Ask what the resonance hybrid of those two forms says about the two carbon-oxygen bonds.

exercises.prompt: Toothpastes containing sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate) and hydrogen peroxide are widely used. Write Lewis structures for the hydrogen carbonate ion and hydrogen peroxide molecule, with resonance forms where appropriate.

answer.solution: In the hydrogen carbonate ion, the carbon atom is bonded to an OH group and two other oxygen atoms. Write a Lewis structure with the section’s procedure, and ask which of the oxygen atoms could carry the double bond to carbon; each possible position gives a resonance form. In hydrogen peroxide, H–O–O–H, every atom reaches its octet or its pair with single bonds only, so ask whether a second structure with the same arrangement of atoms can be written at all.

(a) H3O+
(b) ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$
(c) NH3
(d) ${\text{O}}_{2}{}^{\text{2−}}$
(e) H2O2

answer.solution: Write the Lewis structure of each species first. Then, for each atom, subtract its lone pair electrons and half of its bonding electrons from the number of valence electrons of the free atom, as in Examples 7.6 and 7.7. Check each answer by adding the formal charges: they must total zero for a neutral molecule and the charge of the ion for an ion.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the formal charge of each element in the following compounds and ions:
(a) F2CO
(b) NO–
(c) ${\text{BF}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$
(d) ${\text{SnCl}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$
(e) H2CCH2
(f) ClF3
(g) SeF6
(h) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$

answer.solution: Write the Lewis structure of each species, remembering that some of them, such as ClF<sub>3</sub> and SeF<sub>6</sub>, are exceptions to the octet rule. For each atom, the formal charge is its valence electrons less its lone pair electrons less half of its bonding electrons. The formal charges of each species must add up to its overall charge, which checks the arithmetic.

exercises.prompt: Based on formal charge considerations, which of the following would likely be the correct arrangement of atoms in nitrosyl chloride: ClNO or ClON?

answer.solution: Write a Lewis structure for each arrangement with the section’s procedure and assign the formal charge of every atom. Then apply the guidelines in order: prefer the structure with formal charges of zero, or else the smallest ones, and a negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, as in the choice between the two structures of nitrous oxide.

exercises.prompt: Based on formal charge considerations, which of the following would likely be the correct arrangement of atoms in sulfur dioxide: OSO or SOO?

answer.solution: Write a Lewis structure for each arrangement and assign the formal charge of every atom. Compare the two sets of formal charges with the guidelines, as the section compares the three structures of carbon dioxide: the arrangement with fewer and smaller formal charges, and with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, is the more likely.

exercises.prompt:
Iodine forms a series of fluorides (listed here). Write Lewis structures for each of the four compounds and determine the formal charge of the iodine atom in each molecule:
(a) IF
(b) IF3
(c) IF5
(d) IF7

answer.solution: Iodine is the central atom in each compound, and in IF<sub>3</sub>, IF<sub>5</sub> and IF<sub>7</sub> it is hypervalent, as in the exceptions to the octet rule. Place the fluorine atoms with three lone pairs each and put every remaining electron on the iodine atom. Then count the iodine atom’s lone pair electrons and half of its bonding electrons and subtract both from its seven valence electrons.

answer.solution: NF3;

exercises.prompt: Which of the following structures would we expect for nitrous acid? Determine the formal charges:

answer.solution: Assign the formal charge of every atom in each structure, subtracting its lone pair electrons and half of its bonding electrons from its valence electrons. Then compare the two structures by the guidelines: the one whose formal charges are all zero is preferred.
